corrections.compiler_and_flags: Go 1.7.4 (default go build, GOMAXPROCS set to NP); Intel TBB 2017 Update 3 prebuilt (tbb.lib/tbb.dll, vc14); C++ built with MSVC v14 in Visual Studio 2015 Update 3. The public TBB/TBB.vcxproj at release commit d503e57 sets Release|x64 to Optimization Full (/Ox), IntrinsicFunctions (/Oi), FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed (/Ot), WholeProgramOptimization (/GL), RuntimeLibrary MultiThreaded (/MT) and SDLCheck (/sdl); the Debug|x64 configuration is /Od with tbb_debug.lib. The paper does not say which configuration was measured; the README's run instructions require tbb.dll, which implies the Release build.
corrections.caveats: Single small first-party experiment: one laptop CPU (i7-6700HQ, 4 cores/8 threads), Windows 10, 5 repetitions averaged, 2017 toolchains (Go 1.7.4, TBB 2017U3); raw timings are not in the repo, only figures. The paper's own wording is that TBB was faster in general and Go won only partially at the larger size (N=4096, VP=256 and VP=512, ratio 1.12 and 1.15; the paper does not label the ratio's direction, TBB time over Go time is implied). At N=2048 TBB was faster in every condition and best-vs-best TBB was 1.37x faster. Go's 'superlinear' self-speed-up (6.28 on N=4096, 6.53 in the conclusion) against TBB's 3.95 (4.41) implies a Go sequential run roughly 1.3-1.4x slower than TBB's (derived from page data, assuming the best cases coincide), so the speed-up figures say little about scheduler quality; the two sets of best speed-ups in section 5 and the conclusion also disagree. At VP=2048 Go collapsed (72-91 s at NP=1, 4.9-66.6 s at NP=4) with the Go runtime taking up to 84% of CPU time, attributed to millions of goroutines. The measured build configuration is not stated in the paper; the public vcxproj Release|x64 flags (/Ox /GL) are inferred to be the ones used. The C++ Matrix holds new T[] in a std::unique_ptr<T> (delete instead of delete[]; undefined behaviour at destruction, outside the timed region). The paper is a KIPS (Korea Information Processing Society) conference paper per the release README ('The paper's copyright is reserved by KIPS'); the PDF itself states no venue and peer review of the proceedings is not established. The repo is archived and the README says it is no longer updated; code is under CC-BY-4.0 (not an OSI software licence), so usability is reference. The 2012 Serfass and Tang paper that this repeats is behind a blocked ACM page.
corrections.why_faster: The paper gives no mechanism for Go's win at N=4096 VP=256/512. It only speculates why TBB is generally faster: TBB expresses task dependencies with atomic reference counters and executes the task graph depth-first for cache reuse, while Go's channel-based Dependency.Wait can trigger up to two scheduling events per chunk under the runtime's global run-queue lock. Both sides run the same O(N^3) OBST kernel (Tree::Calculate in C++, Tree.Calculate in Go) over a flat (N+1)^2 matrix with the same VP chunking, so the difference is the runtime and scheduler, not codegen.

notes: Numbers in claimed_speedup all match the PDF (6255.4 vs 12689.6 ms at N=2048; VP=1 6488.6 vs 13266.2 ms; speed-ups 6.28/3.95 and 6.53/4.41; ratios 1.37, 1.12, 1.15). Upgraded to A on the public vcxproj flags, but the build configuration is inferred, not stated: if the orchestrator wants stated flags only, keep C. Record shortcomings: Go faster only in 2 of the measured N=4096 conditions by 1.12-1.15x, TBB faster elsewhere; 2017 toolchains on one laptop; CC-BY-4.0 code, archived. why_faster corrected: the 'cache fit at larger size' explanation is not in the paper. same_opt_level set to true (inferred) in the record keys.

tier_reason: The numbers are an author-posted lock-bench run in the PR conversation (m-ou-se, a Rust libs maintainer, so first-party) on an unnamed '64C/128T AMD Threadripper' with no rustc version or flags; lock-bench (matklad/lock-bench) is public and runs with cargo run --release, but the CPU model and compiler are not given, so it is not A, and nothing independent or peer-reviewed backs it.

corrections.stars_or_usage: 119.7k stars, 18.3k forks (rust-lang/rust); part of the Rust standard library: PR 95035 merged by bors on 2022-04-05, milestone 1.62.0, listed in the 1.62.0 release notes
corrections.caveats: The baseline is the earlier Rust std::sync::Mutex (library/std/src/sys/unix/mutex.rs in 1.60.0): a Box<Mutex> around a pthread_mutex_t initialised as PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL and called through non-inlined libc calls, so part of the gap is the heap indirection rather than glibc's lock algorithm; a C program would normally embed pthread_mutex_t inline, and no standalone C program was benchmarked. glibc's normal mutex is itself a three-state futex lock without spinning, so the new lock's main algorithmic difference is a 100-iteration spin before futex_wait (background knowledge for glibc, not checked in this pass). The run used 32 threads on a 128-thread machine (no oversubscription), which favours spinning: in the same table even spin::Mutex (42.4 ms extreme, 2.13 ms heavy) and AmdSpinlock beat the old glibc-based std Mutex, and parking_lot::Mutex and spin::Mutex were faster than the new std Mutex under light and no contention (parking_lot 0.695 ms and 0.940 ms, spin 0.605 ms and 0.765 ms), while lock-bench's own README on a 4-core i7-7820HQ found spinlocks much worse than a good mutex. Under extreme contention parking_lot (313 ms) was about 11x slower than the new lock. In the 1,000,000-lock no-contention case the old version holds one separately heap-allocated pthread_mutex_t per lock, so its 2.5x gap is mostly memory footprint. Single author-posted run on one machine; the comment itself says 'Realistic benchmarks are very hard'; glibc and musl versions are not stated. rust-timer found no relevant compiler-performance change. lock-bench carries no licence file. Only the Mutex has numbers on the PR page; this PR also replaced Condvar, and the matching RwLock PR (95801) gives none.
corrections.why_faster: PR design (library/std/src/sys/unix/locks/futex.rs in 1.62.0): the lock is one inline AtomicU32 (0 unlocked, 1 locked, 2 contended); lock is a single inlined compare_exchange, a contended lock spins up to 100 times with read-only loads and spin_loop hints before futex_wait, and unlock is one swap that calls futex_wake only when the state was 2. The old std Mutex boxed a pthread_mutex_t (PTHREAD_MUTEX_NORMAL) and called pthread_mutex_lock/unlock in libc through that heap pointer. The contention wins come from spinning before parking on a machine with idle hardware threads, and the no-contention win from removing the boxed per-lock pthread_mutex_t and the libc call; none of it is a Rust codegen effect.

notes: All new-vs-old averages in claimed_speedup match the PR comment tables (27.645506 vs 58.506588/89.146548 ms; 1.822707 vs 8.10534/7.08335 ms; 784.189 us vs 2.802436/2.900143 ms; 1.189231 vs 2.97886/2.794938 ms) and the derived ratios 2.1x, 4.4x, 3.6x, 2.5x check out. Record shortcomings: baseline is glibc pthread_mutex boxed behind Rust std, not a C program; win is lock design (spin, inline futex word), not language; parking_lot and spin beat the new lock under light and no contention; one run, CPU model and compiler unstated.
